name: Sweet potato cultivation in Polynesia
summary: Polynesians were growing sweet potato, a South American crop, in Central Polynesia by about 1200 to 1300 CE, most likely after their own voyagers brought it back across the Pacific.
description: Archaeological finds show that sweet potato, a South American domesticate, had been introduced to Central Polynesia by about 1200 to 1300 CE. Genetic study of herbarium specimens, including plants collected in the Society Islands and New Zealand on Cook's first voyage in 1769, links the Polynesian kumara lineage to the Peru and Ecuador area, and the Polynesian word for the plant resembles the Quechua one. The usual account is that Polynesian voyagers collected it on the west coast of South America about 1000 to 1100 CE and carried it to Hawai'i, Easter Island and New Zealand.

impact.note: One region, Polynesia, took up the crop (reach 1), where it became a main food of the cooler and drier islands such as New Zealand and Easter Island (depth 2), with local cultivation methods as its only known successors (generativity 1); depth rests on general knowledge.

date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

evidence.supports: Archaeological research has now conclusively shown that the sweet potato was introduced to Central Polynesia by approximately A.D. 1200 to 1300

date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Banks and Solander collected sweet potato plants in the Society Islands and New Zealand on Cook's first voyage in 1769; the authors treat them as possibly prehistoric introductions.

evidence.supports: Of salient interest are the specimens collected by J. Banks and D. Solander during Captain James Cook’s first voyage in 1769 (two plants from the Society Islands and one from New Zealand), because they may represent truly prehistoric introductions

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The directly dated remains behind the archaeological date (Hather and Kirch 1991, Mangaia, Cook Islands) were not opened; Denham cites them for the 1200 to 1300 limit.
Whether people carried the crop or it dispersed naturally is disputed; a later genetic study (Muñoz-Rodríguez et al. 2018) argued for natural dispersal and was not opened.
Māori adaptations of cultivation and storage need a source.

research.note: Roullier et al. conclude that the kumara lineage is a pre-Columbian diffusion of sweet potato from the Peru and Ecuador area into Polynesia, and Denham's commentary judges Polynesian voyagers the most likely carriers.
